questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I actually didn't intend on choosing Tasmania. I had missed the first application deadline to apply for other universities in Australia and therefor ended up being able to only choose between Tasmania or Canberra. I chose Tasmania because of the beautiful nature, the cheaper prices, the sense of community and the fact that the UTAS website was very easy to understand and use to search for subjects.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was in SUCH DOUBT about whether or not to do this exchange semester. I was originally going to do it during my Bachelor's degree, but it all got cancelled due to COVID. I didn't think it would be possible to even do this during my Master's, but it all worked out in the end and I could not be more grateful for this experience. I know it's hard work putting this exchange experience together and using the time applying and planning for the semester, but it's 100 % worth it in my opinion. I also had personal reasons for doubting my choice to do this (I was worried about having to do long-distance with my partner), but this was also worth the experience in the end. I learned so much about myself and came back slightly braver and more confident than when I left. I've also experienced what's it's like to study in Australia and made so many new friends along the way. If you are wondering whether or not you should put in the work and hours to plan an exchange semester for yourself, then this is your sign to do it. I loved my life here in Denmark and couldn't really understand why I'd want to leave it all, but wow - this experience has been one of the best times of my life!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Georgia and Patrick at UTAS' Exchange Office are delightful people that are ready to help. They sent a bunch of emails prior to arrival about enrolment and other information. They also sent out a calendar invite link to book a meeting with one of them to just say hi and get acquainted once you arrive. I definitely recommend doing this. They'll buy you coffee and give you all the info you need about orientation week, MyLo, signing up for units, changing units, enrolment deadlines, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The UTAS accommodation office helped me get checked in to the Uni Apartments and the Exchange Coordinators at UTAS reached out and sent a bunch of info my way. As part of living at student accommodation, there was a whole Orientation week and even a P-week prior to that. So basically two full weeks of intro activities that provide campus tours, city tours, get-togethers and barbecues. It was very social and I felt so welcomed and received. Keep in mind I started in February, which is their semester 1.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Definitely join as much O-week related stuff as possible. The accommodation had introduction activities at the same time as the exchange office did, but we kind of just picked and chose what we came to and this worked out great. There are some events that are mandatory though - so keep an eye out for those.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: University apartments, Christ College, Fisher College, Jane Franklin Hall

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: One shared kitchen for the colleges (which seemed very chaotic). If you live in the apartments you only have to share with 5 other people - much nicer. Jane Franklin Hall offers 3 meals a day and full catering service, so no need to worry about grocery shopping or cooking.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Prior to arriving it was a little tricky to know what Uni accommodation I wanted to apply for through UTAS, so here's the breakdown. Fisher and Christ College are like Danish kollegier. Everybody lives on a corridor in a relatively small room - which shared bathrooms in the corridors. There is only one kitchen for all the residents, so it gets busy down there! A lot of first year "freshmen / freshers" live in these colleges, so people are quite young (17-19), but there were quite a few exchange students living there too (21+). I decided to live in a "university appartment" at Sandy Bay campus on college road which is actually also a part of the colleges, but instead of living in tiny dorm rooms, you share a 6-person apartment. This gives you way more space, no cramped kitchen experiences and gives a more "homey" vibe. I definitely recommend these apartments - they have a beautiful view, there's a bus (the unihopper) that can take you in to Hobart and the best part is that you're living with a bunch of other students so it's such a lively and vibrant community. I was 26 during my time in Hobart and the apartments seemed to match my lifestyle and age much better than the colleges. Also, when you arrive, the apartments are just as much a part of the introduction week that is hosted for the colleges! It also feels extremely safe and every time you go for a walk / grocery shopping / out to do your laundry, you always meet somebody you know. Also, the accommodation office is great and every time something needs fixing in the apartments, they'll send somebody to come fix it for you. 
There's also newer and more modern accommodation in Hobart city (Melville Street) but from what I've heard, this is far less social, as students keep to themselves and there's isn't the same "college community vibe". Also more expensive, so I wouldn't say it's worth it. 
The last option for uni accommodation is Jane Franklin Hall. The price seems high, but when you look at the cost breakdown and how much it includes, it would probably be the same as living anywhere elsewhere. Living at Jane would be such an amazing experience - they have a lot of academic help as well as part of their price, so if you're studying law or medicine or other heavy-load courses, then Jane would be a great place to live to take advantage of their tutoring sessions!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Fisher and Christ college have a little bit of a younger age group (17-19 year olds) whereas the Uni apartments are more around (20-mid twenties).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I can't even remember if I had to log in to a portal or if I was just in contact over email with their Exchange Office, but I remember the process as very straightforward. Also, I called them a few times with questions and they were SO helpful over the phone - so don't be shy to reach out to them if you need assistance.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Email correspondence - you can also phone them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The only class I couldn't get was ceramics. This is a very popular elective and I signed up for it quite late. Other than that, I got all the other units that I wanted and I even got to change 3 times during the start of the semester as I realised they weren't as expected. This is very normal and a lot of exchange students do this, so don't worry if you're unsure which units to take - you can most likely "test them out" and decide once you've arrived. You might also have to swap things around if there are timetable clashes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Definitely write all your questions to the people working at the Exchange office of UTAS. They are so kind and helpful and worth reaching out to. Also, make sure your units are actually offered in-person. I had 3 out of 4 units that were online, and this is the only reason I rated my overall experience a 9 out of 10 instead of a 10 out of 10.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My psychology units were super interesting. I had counselling skills and relationship psychology. These were very interesting subjects but they were mainly taught online, which I wasn't a big fan of. There were 2-3 workshops throughout the whole semester, meaning I had very little time in class seeing other people. I gave me COVID vibes to sit in my room or at the library in front of my computer instead of actually having classes to attend. With that said, I did learn a lot. I also took "Health Research Methods CAM720" as a substitute for "Avanceret Metode" and this was a very challenging unit. I do not recommend this unit as it was also online and just such a head-ache to complete.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took 2 units that were on "honors" level - so year 5. This is between a MA and BA, but I was allowed to take these units and the level seemed very appropriate.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They put a lot of emphasis on being able to argument for the points you make in class and in assignments, so be prepared for this. Also, the reading lists (altså pensumlister) for the units are merely suggestions of what to read. It's assumed that you read more or broader than just this list when completing an assignment, so remember to include a bunch of self-found literature! This seems very opposite to KU, so I figured it might be worth mentioning.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
CAM720 - Health research methods 
HEJ509 - Strategic Digital Media
KHA619 - Relationship counselling
KHA609 - Counselling Skills

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I took HEJ509 as a valgfag / elective unit and this was such a blast! It's a hands-on and creative class that doesn't involve much reading, so I really enjoyed the break from heavy academia and the very collaborative classes.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: We rented a car for the duration of our stay from a rental company in Hobart and even though this cost 600 DKK per person (we were 6) per month, it was a GAME CHANGER and almost a MUST in order to explore all the nature and beautiful surroundings around Hobart. Seriously do this. It made the biggest difference. We also had friends that bought a car and sold it before they left for the same price. This also worked out great for them.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Less - Tasmania is so much cheaper than for example Sydney and Melbourne, so I think you save quite a lot of money by going here instead. I'm going to miss the coffees for 25 kroner!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are TONS of clubs in something called TUSA. I didn't participate in these as I was busy with other things. There were also college sports that were quite popular among the people living at the university colleges.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The first intro / orientation week had PLENTY of social activities and if you live at one of the colleges (or the university apartments at College Road), there will be plenty of parties and social events throughout the semester as well.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: See Tasmania! Rent a car and go drive! Our favourite hikes were just 1,5 hours away from Hobart - Cape Hauy and Cape Raoul. Also, there's the Rivulet Track at the base of Mount Wellington which is literally 8 minutes from Hobart. Also, make sure to go camping before the weather gets cold.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
- All the beautiful nature (Cradle Mountain, Mount Wellington, Mount Field, Cape Hauy, Tasman Peninsula, Maria Island, Bruny Island, King Solomon's Cave). 
- Historical & Cultural Sites (Port Arthur, Mona)
- Wildlife Sanctuaries (UnZoo or Bonorong) 
- During winter: Dark Mofo in Hobart

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People are so genuinely friendly and welcoming.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend the barbecues at the start of the semester! I know it's a lot of sausages, but it's a great way to meet new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In the start I was a little shocked at the "style". It's a lot of bare feet, oversized t shirts, mustaches and mullets. But you get used to it, and people are so friendly, even though they look a little rugged.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness, the respect for nature and wildlife, the fact that everybody is so outdoorsy and active in their freetime (rock climbing, mountain biking, bushwalking, hiking, swimming, etc).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Get a car when you arrive (either rent or buy) - this gives you so much freedom and allows you to see 100 times more then if you didn't have one

2. Reach out to the exchange office or accommodation office if you have questions - they are really there to help you!

3. Explore as much of the nature as you can. Tasmania really is STUNNING and there will be so much to see. 

4. Don't overpack, but if you do, you can always go down to the post office in Battery point (much better service then in sandy bay) and send some clothes home. I sent a box with 15 kg of clothes for 1200 DKK - which was far cheaper than having an extra suitcase on the flights home. 

5. Double check that your units are available for in-person teaching. Almost all my classes were online and this was not very fun at all.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Bus: The UniHopper is great to get around if you don't have a car and find yourself living at College Road.

Gym: There is a UniGym at the Sandy Bay campus which is a very basic but effective gym to stay active :) 

Bedding: if you book a room at the College Road Uni apartments, there most likely won't be any bedding when you arrive. I was lucky enough to be provided sheets and a duvet by accommodation, but if not, try go over to the laundry room and check the closets! Other exchange students usually leave their bedding in these. I'd recommend not arriving at night, so that you have time to go to K-mart or Target in town to by bedding and sheets before your first night. 

Doctor's and Insurance: It's compulsory to get a MediBank insurance, but I actually only used my Danish insurance when claiming doctor's visits and blood tests. They reimbursed 100% (I used Europæiske) and this worked much better for me then having to claim via MediBank. Also, if you do get sick, I can recommend the Private Doctor's Clinic at Sandy bay - the appointments are expensive, but if your insurance covers it, then it's worth it! If not, urgent care in Hobart is free (but there's always a 2-4 hour wait).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The fact that I have been dreaming of doing this for so long and finally got to do it. Also the fact that I'm coming home with so many new friendships and life experiences that have matured me as a person.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The fact that most of my classes were online. 
The units I took had quite a heavy workload and I often felt I was juggling a lot of school work compared to at KU. 
I often felt stressed about having to uphold my life in Denmark by catching up and facetiming with friends and family while also having time and energy to meet the new people around me in Tassie.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I really hope this has helped you decide to go to UTAS in Tasmania. It really really really was the experience of a lifetime and well-worth applying for.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
